summary: Edge priority fanout amplification causing intermittent 5xx and streaming drops during tenant concurrency ramp
description: Issue summary: During a tenant concurrency ramp for customer NimbusHealth (dedicated), we observed sustained, intermittent 5xx responses and streaming session drops starting at ~2026-03-13T22:05UTC. The pattern correlated with an edge priority change combined with an automated keystore rotation window. Impact: Multiple production clients reported degraded streaming sessions (short responses, aborted streams) and increased 5xx rate (~8% error-rate for affected tenant traffic) for ~55 minutes. Environment: prod - us-east; affected tenant on Dedicated pool A; traffic spike originated from a scheduled data migration at the customer's side that produced bursty concurrent short requests. Observed behavior: API-Gateway accept queue grew rapidly; hedged/mirrored requests amplified fanout to multiple runtime pools; a transient TLS handshake slowdown during keystore rotation increased handshake latency and caused upstream connection stalls; runtime threadpool utilization went to 95% and a subset of runtime proxies returned 502/503 on request hedged paths. There were frequent short-lived stream disconnects instead of graceful cancelation. This ticket tracks the immediate incident and follow-ups.
steps_to_reproduce: 1) Simulate a high-concurrency ramp from a single tenant with many short streaming requests (concurrency > 1200 per shard)
2) Trigger a keystore rotation (TLS session rehandshake) on the edge proxies during the ramp window
3) Observe accept queue growth in API-Gateway, hedged request fanout increased across serving runtime pools, and rising 502/503 rates for short-streamed sessions
logs: runtime.threadpool.util: 68% -> 95% on pool-c and pool-d at 22:08:30Z
runtime.proxy: upstream reset (RST) on hedged-variant, 502 returned to client (count=1428 in 10m)
comments: Support (Aisha): Customer NimbusHealth opened a support channel. They reported multiple aborted live-transcription sessions. Asked for immediate mitigation and whether a rollback is possible.
SRE (Marco): Initial triage shows accept queue blowup and concurrent TLS latency spike coincident with keystore rotation. Throttled new tenant connections as temporary mitigation.
Customer (NimbusHealth - ops): Confirmed they started a migration job at 22:03 UTC which drastically increased small streaming sessions. Asked whether Redwood can roll back any recent edge change.

SRE (Marco): No recent edge code change deployed around incident time; priority-scheduler tweak was deployed earlier in the day (PR linked). Working hypothesis: scheduler change + keystore rotation + tenant burst caused fanout amplification.

Support (Aisha): Sent customer workaround: reduce client concurrency and enable client-side exponential backoff for short streams; we also recommended pinning to a lower concurrency route (temporary).
Eng (Priya, priority-scheduler): Added logs to track fanout multiplier and hedging counts. Will instrument a circuit to limit simultaneous hedged copies per tenant.
investigation_notes: 00:15 - Correlated timeline: Tenant ramp started 22:03, keystore rotation at 22:05-22:12, error-rate spike 22:06-23:00.
00:30 - Edge metrics show hedged/mirrored request multiplier increased from 1.1x -> 2.6x for affected tenant during high queuing conditions.

00:45 - Keystore rotation led to many edge proxies performing TLS rehandshakes simultaneously; this pushed handshake latencies above the hedging timeout window and caused retried/duplicated hedged requests to be sent upstream.
01:10 - Runtime thread pools were saturated because hedged requests massively increased total inflight token generation work for short-lived sessions (KV cache warmups amplified CPU usage).
01:30 - No evidence of persistent OOMs; runtime recovered after the tenant ramp subsided and keystore rotation completed. Some proxies did perform transient restarts tied to connection resets.
02:00 - Related PR #8241 changed priority-scheduler behavior to be more aggressive in hedging under perceived latency; combined with the keystore rotation this produced the observable amplification.

Suggested root cause: Interaction between aggressive hedging logic in priority-scheduler and simultaneous TLS rehandshake/backpressure from keystore rotation, triggered by an unusually high short-stream concurrency spike from a single tenant.
mitigation_steps_taken: 1) Short-term: Applied tenant-level connection throttle for NimbusHealth to cap concurrency to 600 across affected shards at 22:20 UTC.
2) Disabled hedged request escalation for tenant-level traffic at edge to prevent multi-variant fanout (rolled at 22:35 UTC).
3) Coordinated with infra to stagger keystore rotations and avoid broad simultaneous rehandshake windows (ad hoc scheduling immediate).
4) Customer instructed to pause migration job while throttles in place; customer confirmed decreased error-rate after throttles.
5) Instrumentation: Added metric to track hedged copy count per tenant and per-route (hotfix merged).
resolution_notes: Status: Partial mitigation in place; customer traffic stable with throttles and hedging disabled for affected tenant. Monitoring shows 5xx rate returned to baseline ~30 minutes after throttles.
Next steps (short term): Roll a conservative hedging cap to production-wide policy to limit copies per tenant (ENG- prioritize).
Next steps (mid term): Update keystore rotation orchestration to perform rolling rotations staggered by edge-proxy-subset to avoid clusterwide TLS rehandshake spikes.
Longer term: Rework priority-scheduler hedging logic to factor in accept-queue depth and per-tenant fanout cost (RFC in progress, linked PR and confluence page).
Post-incident: Schedule a brief postmortem with NimbusHealth and internal stakeholders; create runbook entry for tenant-induced burst scenarios and keystore rotation overlap.
Follow-up tickets: INT-2203 (priority-scheduler hedging cap), SUP-421999 (customer-facing postmortem and billing check for retry amplification).
